newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel still sees Germany in EMU after tax blow.
newsitem.headline: Waigel still sees Germany in EMU after tax blow.

text.p: Finance Minister Theo Waigel insisted on Thursday that Germany's chances for joining Europe's single currency on time were unchanged despite a gaping hole torn in his budget by falling tax revenues.

An estimated 18 billion mark ($10.6 billion) shortfall in 1997, the year for judging a country's eligibility for economic and monetary union (EMU), had no fundamental effect on Bonn's prospects, he said in a statement.

But Frankfurt economists said Bonn, which has long insisted on iron-clad guarantees of a stable euro, would probably not now meet the Maastricht deficit criteria meant to ensure the single currency is as strong as the mark.

"(The shortfall) does not lead to a fundamentally different appraisal in relation to the Maastricht criteria," said Waigel, who in a parliamentary debate earlier on Thursday repeated his demand for strict interpretation of the criteria.
Waigel's declaration came only minutes after an expert commission announced the dramatic shortfall in tax revenues, due mainly to record unemployment of about 4.1 million.

As the news broke, the beleaguered finance minister was at the Bundesbank in Frankfurt for what government sources said were talks about whether the central bank could revalue its gold reserves to boost the amount of profits it pays to Bonn.

Revalued gold, sales of Bonn's Deutsche Telekom shares and a government budget freeze are all possible stop-gap measures under feverish discussion in Bonn to plug the budget gaps and help Germany to meet the Maastricht criteria for EMU.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl's centre-right coalition was due to meet on Thursday evening to discuss emergency savings steps.
The Maastricht Treaty says countries joining EMU should have budget deficits no higher than three percent of gross domestic product and overall debts not more than 60 percent of GDP.
Economists said the huge tax shortfall meant Waigel might well miss his own targets.

"Germany will certainly not make the 3.0 percent deficit criterion," said Stefan Schneider at Paribas in Frankfurt. "He will have to eat his words and say that a number slightly above three percent will be fine too."
Holger Schmieding of Merrill Lynch said: "It looks like we will not make it." UBS's Ralf Kugelstadt said Bonn damaged its own credibility by casting its eyes on Bundesbank gold.
"This is not at all what the Bundesbank and the government itself have called for from other countries," Kugelstadt said. "They spoke against one-off measures."

The tax revenue shortfall means Waigel has 18 billion marks less than he planned for in his 1997 budget, which set the budget deficit at 2.5 percent to give Bonn leeway if -- as has now happened -- it needs to spend more to combat joblessness.
The tax commission said it also expected 1998 tax income for federal, state and local governments would be 31.6 billion marks below what Bonn had until now assumed.
Waigel said in his statement that the shortfall meant Germany should forge ahead with plans for a broad tax reform, including a drop in the peak personal tax rate of 53 percent.

In parliament, Waigel came out firmly against any weakening in the Maastricht criteria, saying: "Convergence determines the timetable, for every country." Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt firmly opposed a delay in launching the euro.
Afterwards, Kohl's majority defeated an opposition motion calling for an active jobs policy in the "stability pact" meant to guarantee the euro's value.
Opposition Social Democrats (SPD) threatened to reject the revised Maastricht treaty to be approved at the EU's Amsterdam summit in June if it had no active European jobs policy.

But speakers from the SPD and ecologist Greens party also strongly supported the euro, arguing that a stable single currency was urgently needed to support German exports and help the EU avoid the worst effects of currency speculation.

Strategists for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) said they considered the SPD threat a tactical move and did not expect the strongly pro-European party to waver when parliamentary approval is needed to join EMU.
